head: Not this

rows: Tennyson uses rhythm. It is fast. Satyamurti uses first person. It is personal.
Tennyson's rhythm rushes the reader forward with the crowd, whereas Satyamurti's first person slows us down with one witness.

model.title: Compare how the poets present thinking about war.

parts.text: P: both poems ask whether people may question war
E: 'Theirs not to reason why' / a line where the photographer reflects
M and A: Tennyson's command-like repetition vs a reflective first person
C and S: Victorian duty vs modern conscience: questioning has become part of witnessing

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: Tennyson's soldiers are forbidden to 'reason why', whereas Satyamurti's photographer cannot stop reasoning: the shift from a commanding refrain to a reflective first-person voice suggests that, for a modern witness, questioning war has become a duty.

questions.q: Weave: 'Tennyson uses a refrain. Satyamurti looks back on one moment.'
questions.a: For example: 'Tennyson's refrain returns again and again to the charge, whereas Satyamurti's speaker returns again and again to one moment.'

questions.q: Add a Significance sentence to the woven example
questions.a: For example: 'This matters because it shows war's cost repeats in memory long after the event.'
